messages.body_plain:
parallel E-step available: https://github.com/dji-transpire/mirt/tree/parallel-estep
This branch provides a parallel E-step for mirt that is much faster than serial execution on a single core. It uses all cores by default.
The local ~/.R/Makevars must to include the -fopenmp option. Here are the contents I use:
CFLAGS +=              -O3 -Wall -pipe -pedantic -std=gnu99  -fopenmp
CXXFLAGS +=            -O3 -Wall -pipe -Wno-unused -pedantic -fopenmp

Technical details on the parallel-E parallel-M algorithm can be found here

von Davier, M. (2016), High‐Performance Psychometrics: The Parallel‐E Parallel‐M Algorithm for Generalized Latent Variable Models. ETS Research Report Series, 2016: 1-11.  https://doi.org/10.1002/ets2.12120

and here

von Davier M. (2017) New Results on an Improved Parallel EM Algorithm for Estimating Generalized Latent Variable Models. In: van der Ark L.A., Wiberg M., Culpepper S.A., Douglas J.A., Wang WC. (eds) Quantitative Psychology. IMPS 2016. Springer Proceedings in Mathematics & Statistics, vol 196. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-56294-0_1

Hi Caio,

If you have the original data then what is stopping you from estimating the item parameter directly via mirt()? Again, I would advise against using previously saved point estimates since these are a) sub-optimal, in that they are either positively or negatively biased, and b) do not account for the sampling/measurement precision that was originally present (this is actually the main problem with a selection of item-fit statistics that rely on point estimates). No doubt if your estimation is the same as the original calibration then you'd be able to obtain the same latent trait point estimates anyway as a consequence, rendering your current point estimates redundant anyway.

Phil

Hi Conrad,

Sorry for the delay; life is pretty wild right now now at home/work (a line that's pretty blurry these days....). There's various ways that I can answer this question, so I might need more background information. Are you trying to make a CAT implementation yourself, or are you just trying to track how theta changes over time in a more interest-sake way? If the latter, you can just use mirt::fscores() and supply an observed pattern to the response.pattern input, which mostly will consist of NA placeholders for items that have no response. If the former, functions like updateDesign() showcase how one can explore some of the internally manipulated functions used in calls to mirtCAT() in a more interactive way, though what you are looking for may require a bit more exposure of the specific internals (I've chosen not to export everything for front-end users to play with since things could get complicated very quickly). messages.body_plain:
Hi Caio,

I see your problem. However, using the point estimates of the latent traits as provisionally known certainly won't give you the original item parameter estimates (it's not synonymous to a back-transformation operation). You'd likely get very different parameter estimates since the individual point estimates will have a very different mean/variance combination than the original calibration method (most likely mean-variance = 0-1). If you have multiple set of plausible values for the latent traits (which in some sense 'retain' the original identification constraints) then those could do a better job when averaged over, but even here they won't be perfect. IN any event, using only the subset data that you have available will likely give you much closer representations to the original data than any set of latent trait point estimates since the data are (presumably) both random samples from the same population.

Phil

xsi = 21-40

Thanks for your support.

messages.body_plain:
Using multiple group IRT and concurrent calibration should provide the most rigorous linking of IRT scales across populations. This works with multiple test forms and across multiple population as long as each form is connected to other forms through link items, which can be complex connections or linkages. Fixed parameter linking is also possible. And in the worst case, parameters can be transformed to match certain targets such as averages of item difficulties and slopes from other forms. Common population linking is also straight forward.
